entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 3 THE POEM OR DEBATE ITSELF (Job 3:2-42:6). FIRST SERIES IN IT (Job 3: 1-14:22 ). JOB FIRST ( Job 3:1-26 ). Job 3:1-19 . Job Curses the Day of His Birth and Wishes for Death. 1. opened his mouth-- The Orientals speak seldom, and then sententiously; hence this formula expressing deliberation and gravity ( Psa 78:2 ). He formally began. cursed his day-- the strict Hebrew word for "cursing:" not the same as in Job 1:5 . Job cursed his birthday, but not his God.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4492"/><div sID="gen6509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4492"/><hi type="bold">2. spake--</hi>Hebrew, "answered," that is, not to any actual question that preceded, but to the question virtually involved in the case. His outburst is singularly wild and bold (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.14">Jr 20:14</reference>). To desire to die so as to be free from sin is a mark of grace; to desire to die so as to escape troubles is a mark of corruption. He was ill-fitted to die who was so unwilling to live. But his trials were greater, and his light less, than ours. <div eID="gen6509" type="x-p"/>

Let ... the shadow of death--</hi>("deepest darkness," <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Is 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen6512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stain it--</hi>This is a later sense of the verb [Gesenius]; better the old and more poetic idea, "Let darkness (the ancient night of chaotic gloom) resume its rights over light (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Ge 1:2</reference>), and claim that day as its own."<div eID="gen6513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a cloud--</hi>collectively, a gathered mass of dark clouds.<div eID="gen6514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the blackness of the day terrify it--</hi>literally, "the obscurations"; whatever darkens the day [Gesenius]. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4498"/><div sID="gen6519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4498"/><hi type="bold">8. them ... curse the day--</hi>If "mourning" be the right rendering in the latter clause of this verse, these words refer to the hired mourners of the dead (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.17">Jr 9:17</reference>). But the Hebrew for "mourning" elsewhere always denotes an animal, whether it be the crocodile or some huge serpent (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>), such as is meant by "leviathan." Therefore, the expression, "cursers of day," refers to magicians, who were believed to be able by charms to make a day one of evil omen. (So Balaam, <reference osisRef="Num.22.5">Nu 22:5</reference>). This accords with Umbreit's view (<reference osisRef="Job.3.7">Job 3:7</reference>); or to the Ethiopians and Atlantes, who "used to curse the sun at his rising for burning up them and their country" [Herodotus]. Necromancers claimed power to control or rouse wild beasts at will, as do the Indian serpent-charmers of our day (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.5">Psa 58:5</reference>). Job does not say they had the power they claimed; but, supposing they had, may they curse the day. Schuttens renders it by supplying words as follows:--Let those that are ready for anything, call it (the day) the raiser up of leviathan, that is, of a host of evils. <div eID="gen6519" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4502"/><div sID="gen6523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4502"/><hi type="bold">14. With kings ... which built desolate places for themselves--</hi>who built up for themselves what proved to be (not palaces, but) ruins! The wounded spirit of Job, once a great emir himself, sick of the vain struggles of mortal great men, after grandeur, contemplates the palaces of kings, now desolate heaps of ruins. His regarding the repose of death the most desirable end of the great ones of earth, wearied with heaping up perishable treasures, marks the irony that breaks out from the black clouds of melancholy [Umbreit]. The "for themselves" marks their selfishness. Michaelis explains it weakly of mausoleums, such as are found still, of stupendous proportions, in the ruins of Petra of Idumea. <div eID="gen6523" type="x-p"/>
